blocks.text: But to make the whole matter clearer, I must say a few things first about the charming of serpents. Augustine ^{a)} holds that serpents are moved by the songs of men more than any other kind of animal, so that this would be a proof that the first man was seduced by the devil through the serpent in Paradise. And so you may see whole nations notorious for this kind of enchantment. Among them are the Marsi and the Psylli, as everyone knows. But you may also read in Aelian, History book 6, chapter 33, that the Egyptians do the same μαγείᾳ τινὶ ἐπιχωρίῳ [mageia tini epichōriō], by a certain magical art peculiar to that nation. And the Nubian Geographer, first Clime, part 7, reports this very thing of the people of Melinde: يزعمون انهم يسحرون الحيوان الضار حتي لا يضر الا لمن ارادوا ضره [yazʿumūn annahum yasḥarūn al-ḥayawān al-ḍārr ḥattā lā yaḍurr illā li-man arādū ḍarrahu] They are said to charm noxious animals so that they harm no one except whom they themselves wish. And Cadamosto of the Negroes: There are also enchanters, that is, outstanding charmers. They enchant serpents above all. And Spitillus in his Collectanea of the Peruvians in the New World: At festival time a boy, crowned, with a spear in one hand and a live viper hanging from the other, takes a seat placed in a very richly adorned spot. From this it is easily inferred that these are arts of the demon, since he is not bitten by the viper. And Teixeira of the Indians, History of Persia book 1, chapter 29: Los vemos comunmente en la India adò suelen los gentiles traher culebras encantadas, algunes muy grandes, y terribles, por las calles, y casas, haziendo las baylar al son de una flauta, y las rebuelven al cuello, y hazen con ellas otros semejantes ademanes, tratando las con las manos sin [III, 163] offensa suya. Y aunque algunos los attribuen a no tener dientes, porque dizen se los sacan siendo chiquitas. La experienzia muestra lo contrario, puez siendo algunas vezes ensannadas, o no tan ligadas con el encanto como convenia, se ha visto, que hazian grande estrago en los aspectantes. In Latin this runs: We have often seen this in India, where the heathen are accustomed to lead charmed serpents, some of them very large and terrible, through the streets and houses; they handle them unharmed, make them dance to the sound of a pipe, twist them round the neck, and perform other gestures of this kind. Some keep saying this happens because they are toothless, and that their teeth, which are small, are easily pulled out. But those who think so are refuted by experience, since these same serpents, when provoked and not bound by the charm as firmly as they should be, have sometimes been seen to cause great slaughter among the spectators ^{(2)}.

Nor was this superstition born today or yesterday. You may see traces of it everywhere in the most ancient writers. Thus Orpheus is fabled to have recalled Eurydice, struck by a serpent, from the underworld, because

— — ὑπὸ ὄφεως αὐτὴν τῷ ὄντι δεδηγμένην Καὶ κυνδυνεύσαν θανεῖν, ταῖς ἐπῳδαῖς, αἷς οἶδε, Καὶ ἀγχινοίᾳ, μέσῃ τε, καὶ πολυμαθείᾳ Αὐτὴν ἐζωοποίησεν· — — — — [— — hypo opheōs autēn tō onti dedēgmenēn / Kai kyndyneusan thanein, tais epōdais, hais oide, / Kai anchinoia, mesē te, kai polymatheia / Autēn ezōopoiēsen · — — — —]

She had in truth been bitten by a snake and was in danger of her life; by the incantations he knew, by his skill, his muse and his great learning he restored her to life. So Tzetzes, Chiliad 2, History 54. And the same writer proves that this art was not unknown to Orpheus [III, 164] from the words of Orpheus himself in the work On Stones (a work which, however, I would rather ascribe with Suidas to Timocles of Syracuse),
Ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι χαμαὶ ἐρχομένοιο δράκοντος, Εἴσεται, ἠδ' ὄφεων ἰὸν σβέσαι ἑρπυστήρων· [Rhoizon te stēsai chamai erchomenoio drakontos, / Eisetai, ēd' opheōn ion sbesai herpystērōn ·]

He will know how to stop the hissing of the dragon coming along the ground, and to quench the poison (or rather the dart) of creeping serpents. I cite these words the more gladly because Paul plainly alludes to them in Ephes. VI, 16. You will find them, moreover, in the proem of the work Περὶ [col. 387] λίθων [Peri lithōn], but corrupted. For instead of ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι [rhoizon te stēsai], our editions, against both metre and sense, have Ῥοιζῶντες, καὶ [Rhoizōntes, kai], etc. To the same point belongs what we read of Medea in Apollonius, Argonautica book 4, line 147:
Ἡδείῃ ἐνοπῇ θέλξαι τέρας, [Hēdeiē enopē thelxai teras,]
that she soothed the monster with sweet voice, that is, the dragon, guardian of the golden fleece. Accordingly there follows not much later,
— — — αὐτὰρ ὅ γ' ἤδη Οἴμῃ θελγόμενος δολιχὴν ἀναλύετ᾽ ἄκανθαν, [— — — autar ho g' ēdē / Oimē thelgomenos dolichēn analyet' akanthan,]
So, soothed by her song, his long spine was relaxed. But Ovid, ascribing the same thing to Jason in book 7 of the Metamorphoses:
After he had sprinkled him with herbs of Lethean juice, And thrice spoken the words that bring peaceful sleep.
